script.opening: “Hello doctor. So the bloods were all normal again. I don’t understand — something is obviously wrong with me. I really think I need a proper scan, a full-body MRI, to find out what’s causing it.”

facts.text: “It’s everywhere — neck, shoulders, back, hips, even my arms and legs. It moves about. A deep ache, burning sometimes. It’s been about a year and a half.” Worse after a busy day and when stressed or cold.
“I’m in bed by nine and wake up like I haven’t slept. My head’s foggy — I lose words at work.”
“Stiff for maybe twenty minutes in the morning.” No swollen joints, no hot joints, no rashes, no mouth ulcers, no dry eyes or mouth, no hair loss, no fevers.
“Sometimes my hands feel tingly but it comes and goes, both hands.” No weakness, no loss of vision or double vision, no walking or balance problems, no bladder or bowel changes.
No weight loss, no night sweats. Appetite fine. Muscles not weak — “I can lift things, it just hurts”.

“The co-codamol takes the edge off. I’m taking two, four times a day now — every day.” If asked about headaches: “I get a headache most mornings, so I take two more.” Constipated, which you put down to IBS.
“I’m fed up and weepy. I used to love walking the dog.” If asked about harming yourself: “No — I’d never do that. I just want my life back.”
Full-time school administrator. Eight days off sick this term. “I’ve got an attendance review meeting next Thursday. I’m terrified I’ll lose my job.” (Say this only if work is explored.)
Married, two teenagers. If asked how your husband feels: “Paul thinks it’s all in my head. That I just need to get on with it.” (Upset.)

facts.topic: Your fear (only if asked what you’re worried it is)
facts.text: “My cousin has MS. She started with aches and tiredness and they kept telling her it was nothing.”

Start frustrated and a little defensive. If the doctor dismisses you or says “all your tests are normal, so there’s nothing wrong”, become upset and insist on the MRI. If they ask what you fear, tell them about your cousin. If they explain the condition in a way that believes you and takes the MS fear seriously, soften and accept a plan without a scan. You are reluctant about exercise but open to it if it is graded and supervised. You are worried about stopping co-codamol (“it’s the only thing that helps”) but will agree to a slow reduction.

ice.ideas: “Something is being missed — a scan will find it.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — her cousin has multiple sclerosis that was dismissed for years; she fears the same. She is also frightened of losing her job at next week’s attendance meeting, and hurt that her husband says it is “all in her head”.
ice.expectations: A full-body MRI; at least a referral to a specialist “who will take me seriously”.

cues: “Something is obviously wrong with me.” — needs validation before explanation.
“They kept telling her it was nothing.” (if she mentions her cousin) — the MS fear.
“I’ve got a meeting at work next week.” — the practical crisis.

checkpoints.text: Takes a focused pain history and screens for alternative diagnoses: inflammatory arthritis, connective tissue disease, PMR, myositis (CK normal), hypothyroidism, neurological symptoms (MS features), weight loss or night sweats
Uses the normal bloods and the physiotherapy findings already available, and explores sleep, fatigue, cognition, mood (including suicidal thoughts) and the impact on work and home
Identifies daily co-codamol use with morning headaches as probable medication-overuse headache and opioid harm
Makes and names a positive diagnosis — fibromyalgia, a type of chronic primary pain — rather than a diagnosis of exclusion
Explains why an MRI would not help (and the harm of incidental findings), while addressing the specific MS fear with the features that would change that

Offers NICE-consistent options: supervised graded exercise, psychological therapy (CBT or ACT), acupuncture as an option, and an antidepressant option with benefits and harms; does not start gabapentinoids, opioids, NSAIDs or benzodiazepines

Agrees a gradual co-codamol taper, supports work (fit note “may be fit for work” with adjustments, occupational health), and arranges review with safety-netting for new neurological or inflammatory features
Validates the pain as real, explores the husband’s view and the work meeting, and builds a shared plan she believes in

worked.txt: “Your pain is real. Normal blood tests don’t mean nothing is wrong — they tell us what it isn’t, and that matters too.”
“When you imagine what the scan might show, what are you most worried about?”

“This pattern has a name — fibromyalgia. It’s a condition where the nervous system’s pain volume is turned up, so normal signals are felt as pain. It’s diagnosed by its pattern, which you have, not by a scan.”

“The things that make me think of MS — loss of vision, double vision, weakness in a limb, trouble walking or with your bladder — you haven’t had any. If any of those happened, I’d want to see you quickly, and that’s when a scan helps.”
“Codeine every day can actually cause the morning headaches, and it doesn’t work well for this kind of pain over time. I’d like us to cut it down slowly together — not stop it suddenly.”
“Let’s get you ready for Thursday — a fit note saying you may be fit for work with adjustments, and a letter about the diagnosis, could help your manager understand.”

f.learning: Chronic widespread pain with fatigue, unrefreshing sleep and cognitive symptoms, normal inflammatory markers, thyroid and CK, and no synovitis or neurological signs is fibromyalgia — classified by NICE as chronic primary pain. The skill is a positive, validating diagnosis after a targeted screen for alternatives (inflammatory arthritis, connective tissue disease, PMR over 50, myositis, hypothyroidism, neurological disease, malignancy features), not a diagnosis of exclusion delivered as “there’s nothing wrong”. Address the specific fear (here MS) by naming the features that would change the plan; more imaging finds incidental abnormalities and reinforces illness worry. NICE recommends supervised group exercise programmes, psychological therapies (CBT or ACT), acupuncture within a defined course, and considering an antidepressant (amitriptyline, citalopram, duloxetine, fluoxetine, paroxetine or sertraline) for pain, quality of life and sleep after discussing benefits and harms. Do not start opioids, gabapentinoids or other antiepileptics, NSAIDs, paracetamol, benzodiazepines, antipsychotics or ketamine for chronic primary pain; if she is already taking them, review and agree a shared, gradual reduction. Daily codeine with morning headaches suggests medication-overuse headache. Screen mood and suicidal thoughts; support work with a fit note and adjustments.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG193 Chronic pain (primary and secondary) in over 16s: assessment of all chronic pain and management of chronic primary pain (2021) · EULAR revised recommendations for the management of fibromyalgia (2016; international) · NICE NG215 Medicines associated with dependence or withdrawal symptoms (2022) · NICE CG150 Headaches in over 12s: diagnosis and management (2012, updated 2021) · DWP Getting the most out of the fit note: guidance for healthcare professionals (2022)
knowledge.summary: Believe, screen, name it positively, explain why a scan will not help, and offer exercise, psychological therapy and an antidepressant option — while tapering the co-codamol.

points.t: Widespread pain for 3 months or more, fatigue, unrefreshing sleep and cognitive symptoms, with normal ESR/CRP, FBC, TSH, CK, bone profile and no synovitis. The 2016 ACR criteria (widespread pain index and symptom severity) support a clinical diagnosis; tender-point counting is no longer required.

Inflammatory arthritis (morning stiffness over 30–60 minutes, joint swelling), connective tissue disease (rash, ulcers, sicca, Raynaud’s), PMR (over 50, proximal stiffness, raised ESR), myositis (weakness, raised CK — statins), hypothyroidism, neurological disease (focal deficits), malignancy (weight loss, night sweats, bone pain), and depression.

Supervised group exercise programmes; psychological therapies (CBT, ACT); acupuncture within a single course; and an antidepressant after discussing benefits and harms — amitriptyline at night (10 mg, titrate) or duloxetine are often chosen. Sleep hygiene and pacing.

points.h: What NICE says not to start
points.t: Opioids, gabapentinoids and other antiepileptics, NSAIDs, paracetamol, benzodiazepines, antipsychotics, local anaesthetic or steroid trigger-point injections, ketamine. For someone already taking them: explain the lack of evidence, then agree a shared, gradual reduction.

Reduce by about 10–25% of the dose every 1–2 weeks (for example 8 → 6 → 4 → 2 → 0 tablets daily), using the paracetamol component alone briefly if needed; warn of transient worsening of pain and headache; review weekly to fortnightly. Medication-overuse headache improves after withdrawal.

A fit note can say “may be fit for work” with phased return, altered hours or adjusted duties. Suggest an occupational health referral via her employer; reasonable adjustments may apply if the condition has a long-term substantial effect.
The pass is the positive diagnosis and a plan without scans or new analgesics. The Clear pass finds the MS fear and the work crisis and changes the plan because of them.

model.text: Hello Joanne, I’m Dr Mensah. I’ve seen your blood results and the physio letter. Before I go through them, tell me how things are for you at the moment.
model.why: Open question; signals the records have been read

model.text: Awful. The bloods were all normal again. Something is obviously wrong. I really think I need a full-body MRI.
I can hear how frustrating that is — you feel unwell, and “normal” doesn’t feel like an answer. Can you tell me about the pain itself?
It’s everywhere, it moves about, deep ache, burning. Eighteen months now. And I’m exhausted, my head’s foggy.
Any swollen or hot joints, stiffness for more than half an hour in the morning, rashes, mouth ulcers, dry eyes, weight loss or night sweats?
model.why: Screens for inflammatory and systemic disease

model.text: Stiff maybe twenty minutes. None of the rest.
Any weakness, numbness in one area, changes to your vision, double vision, problems walking or with your bladder?
My hands tingle sometimes, both of them. Nothing else. Why do you ask that?
I’m checking for things that would need a different plan. When you picture what a scan might show, what worries you most?
My cousin has MS. They told her it was nothing for years.
That makes complete sense of wanting a scan. Can I ask how you’re managing the pain day to day — and how your mood is?
Co-codamol, two, four times a day. I get a headache most mornings so I take more. I’m weepy. Not suicidal — I just want my life back.
And how is this affecting work and home?
Attendance meeting next Thursday. Paul thinks it’s all in my head.

I believe you, and it’s not in your head the way Paul means. This pattern — widespread pain, exhaustion, poor sleep, foggy thinking, with normal tests — is called fibromyalgia. The nerves that carry pain have their volume turned up. It’s diagnosed by the pattern, which you have.

About MS: the signs that would point there — losing vision, double vision, a weak limb, trouble walking or with your bladder — you haven’t had. An MRI now would likely show small, unimportant findings that cause more worry. If any of those signs appear, I’d see you quickly and scan.
model.why: Explains why not to scan; targeted safety-net

model.text: So what can actually help?

The things with the best evidence are a supervised exercise programme that starts very gently, talking therapy that helps you live with pain, and there’s also the option of acupuncture or a medicine like amitriptyline at night that can help pain and sleep. Which of those appeals?
model.why: NICE NG193 options offered for shared choice

model.text: Amitriptyline for sleep, and maybe the exercise if it’s gentle. But not stopping the co-codamol.

Codeine every day can cause those morning headaches and doesn’t help this pain long term. Let’s cut it slowly — six tablets a day for a fortnight, then four — and I’ll check in with you each time. For Thursday, I’ll do a fit note saying you may be fit for work with adjustments, and suggest occupational health.
model.why: Shared opioid taper and work support

model.text: Would it help if Paul came to the next appointment so we can explain it together? Tell me what you’ll take away from today.
It’s called fibromyalgia, it’s real, no scan unless I get those nerve symptoms, amitriptyline, physio class, cut the co-codamol slowly. And yes — bring Paul.

social.t: A partner who believes it is “all in her head” undermines recovery. A joint appointment with consent can reframe it as a real, explainable condition.
Attendance management is a crisis point; a fit note with adjustments and occupational health advice can protect employment.

legal.t: If the condition has a substantial and long-term effect on day-to-day activities, the employer may need to make reasonable adjustments.

professional.t: Imaging without a clinical question generates incidental findings and anxiety. Explaining why a test is not needed is a skill, not a refusal.
A locum’s opioid becomes your responsibility at review. NICE advises reviewing and reducing medicines that are not helping chronic primary pain.

community.t: Local pain management or ESCAPE-pain type programmes; NHS Talking Therapies for long-term conditions; Versus Arthritis and Fibromyalgia Action UK information.

redFlags: Joint swelling, prolonged morning stiffness, rash, ulcers, sicca
Focal neurology, visual loss, bladder symptoms
ice: Concern: MS like her cousin; losing her job
core: Distribution, duration and character of pain

playbook.diagnosis: Fibromyalgia (chronic primary pain) with probable medication-overuse headache from daily co-codamol.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your pain system has become over-sensitive — like a smoke alarm that goes off when you make toast. The pain is real, but it isn’t caused by damage a scan would show.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted a scan because your cousin’s MS was missed. You don’t have the signs of MS, and I’ve told you exactly what would make me scan.”
management.psychosocial: Fit note and occupational health for Thursday; offer a joint appointment with Paul.
sharedPlan: Psychological therapy (CBT or ACT) via Talking Therapies
Gradual co-codamol taper with fortnightly review
Fit note “may be fit for work” with adjustments
safetyNet: Urgent review if visual loss, double vision, limb weakness, walking or bladder problems
Review for joint swelling, rash, weight loss or fevers
Seek help if mood worsens or thoughts of self-harm

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed either by ordering the scan to end the conflict, or by a cold “your tests are normal” that leaves her unheard.

items.fail: “All your tests are normal, so there’s nothing seriously wrong.”
items.why: It sounds like disbelief; she escalates and the plan collapses.
items.fix: Validate the pain, then give a positive diagnosis with a clear explanation.

items.fail: Adds pregabalin or increases codeine to “give her something”.
items.why: NICE advises against starting gabapentinoids or opioids for chronic primary pain; harms outweigh benefits.
items.fix: Offer exercise, psychological therapy, acupuncture or an antidepressant, and taper the opioid.

items.fail: Never asks what she fears the scan will show, so the MS worry is never answered.
items.why: Unaddressed fear drives repeat attendance and investigation requests.
items.fix: Ask the fear, then name the specific features that would change the plan.

timeMap.d: Let her say she wants the MRI; acknowledge the frustration.
Inflammatory, neurological and systemic red flags; analgesia; mood; work; husband; the fear.
Positive diagnosis of fibromyalgia; why no scan; MS features to watch for.
Exercise, therapy, amitriptyline or other options; co-codamol taper; fit note.
Teach-back, joint appointment with Paul, review date.

wordPics.clearFail: Orders an MRI or refers to rheumatology simply to satisfy the request, or dismisses her; adds pregabalin or more opioid; no mood screen.
wordPics.fail: Gives a vague “it may be fibromyalgia, try exercise” without exploring the fear or the codeine use; plan she does not believe.
wordPics.pass: Screens appropriately, names fibromyalgia positively, explains why no scan, offers NICE options and a co-codamol taper, and safety-nets for neurological features.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the Pass, plus uncovers and answers the MS fear specifically, spots medication-overuse headache, supports her for the work meeting, invites Paul, and she leaves feeling believed with a plan she chose.

avoid.instead: “Your tests show what it isn’t — and the pattern tells us what it is.”
avoid.why: Normal tests are reassuring only when paired with a positive explanation.

avoid.instead: “Stress and poor sleep can turn the pain volume up, but the pain is real.”
avoid.why: Attributing it to stress alone feels dismissive and echoes her husband.

avoid.dont: “Let’s just do the MRI to put your mind at rest.”
avoid.instead: “A scan would likely find small things that don’t matter and worry you more. Here’s what would make me scan.”
avoid.why: Reassurance scans rarely reassure and can cause harm.

dg.d: Open question; lets Joanne describe 18 months of widespread pain, fatigue and poor sleep and what she hopes a scan would show.
School administrator with an attendance meeting next week, husband who says it is “all in her head”, sleep, mood, cousin with MS.
Uses the normal bloods (inflammatory markers, TFT, CK, calcium, vitamin D, coeliac, ferritin) and physio findings; no MRI without new neurological or inflammatory signs.
Fibromyalgia vs inflammatory arthritis, connective tissue disease, PMR, myositis, hypothyroidism, MS; identifies medication-overuse headache from co-codamol.
Screens neurological (MS) features, synovitis, weight loss and night sweats; asks about mood and suicidal thoughts; recognises opioid harm.
Names a positive diagnosis — fibromyalgia, a type of chronic primary pain — plus probable medication-overuse headache, not “nothing wrong”.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: NICE NG193 options: supervised exercise, CBT or ACT, acupuncture, an antidepressant option; no gabapentinoids, opioids, NSAIDs or benzodiazepines; explains why no MRI.
Agreed gradual co-codamol taper (also treats the headache); sleep and mood; fit note “may be fit” with adjustments, occupational health; offers to involve her husband.
Review in a few weeks; safety-net for new neurological symptoms, joint swelling, weight loss or worsening mood or suicidal thoughts.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Follows “something is obviously wrong with me”, “they kept telling her it was nothing” (her cousin) and “a meeting at work next week”.
Idea (something missed; a scan will find it); concern (MS like her cousin, her job, not being believed); expectation (full-body MRI or a specialist).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — her cousin has multiple sclerosis that was dismissed for years; she fears the same. She is also frightened of losing her job at next week’s attendance meeting, and hurt that her husband says it is “all in her head” — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.
